power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Over the past three decades, mentalization theory has captured the imagination and curiosity of clinicians, researchers, educators, and professionals across a broad range of disciplines.
Alongside its growing influence, questions concerning the definition and measurement of mentalizing as a target construct have remained a recurring theme in literature.
This raises two related questions: what are we measuring when we assess mentalizing, and what is the empirical basis for conceptualizing it as a four-dimensional construct?

The four-dimensional formulation assumes that four distinct dimensions can be identified and measured, that their polarities form meaningful continuum, that balance and imbalance can be defined, and that the dimensions together form a coherent psychological structure.
We propose distinguishing between the assessment of the mentalization theory and of mentalizing itself as a target construct.
Adopting a curious, not-knowing stance, we revisit these assumptions and invite further consideration of the architecture and measurement of the mentalizing target construct.

The process whereby one human mind supports another by providing understanding, organization, processing, and clarification of mental states has been described as a central process since the early days of psychology (Bion, 1962a).
text.formatted: The process whereby one human mind supports another by providing understanding, organization, processing, and clarification of mental states has been described as a central process since the early days of psychology <ref type="bibr">(Bion, 1962a)</ref>.

text.text: Mentalization has become an increasingly influential construct in clinical psychology, as well as across broad areas of psychological research (Ballespí et al., 2018; Cosenza et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Mentalization has become an increasingly influential construct in clinical psychology, as well as across broad areas of psychological research <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ballespí et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cosenza et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, despite several decades of theoretical and empirical work, a fundamental question concerning measurement remains open: what exactly is being measured when we measure mentalization?
A growing number of measurement instruments approach mentalization from different theoretical assumptions, although in most cases there is only partial overlap (Hawksdale et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A growing number of measurement instruments approach mentalization from different theoretical assumptions, although in most cases there is only partial overlap <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hawksdale et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, the four-dimensional model commonly used to describe mentalization has provided an influential clinical framework, but its proposed multidimensional structure has yet to receive clear empirical validation.
These questions are not new.

After more than three decades of research on mentalization, the need for measurement instruments that reflect the fourdimensional model continues to be raised in different articles (Dimitrijević et al., 2018; Gagliardini et al., 2018; Gori et al., 2021).
text.formatted: After more than three decades of research on mentalization, the need for measurement instruments that reflect the fourdimensional model continues to be raised in different articles <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dimitrijević et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gagliardini et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Gori et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: We would like to take a step back and ask whether there is room to reconsider the target construct of mentalization.

The claim that mentalization is organized along four bipolar dimensions has become a familiar assumption that routinely appears in the mentalization literature (Fonagy & Luyten, 2009; Luyten & Fonagy, 2015; Luyten et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The claim that mentalization is organized along four bipolar dimensions has become a familiar assumption that routinely appears in the mentalization literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fonagy & Luyten, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Luyten & Fonagy, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Luyten et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The polarities of the mentalization dimensions provide the framework through which we can understand the relationships between mentalization theory and other overlapping constructs (Fonagy, Bateman, & Bateman, 2011).
text.formatted: The polarities of the mentalization dimensions provide the framework through which we can understand the relationships between mentalization theory and other overlapping constructs <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fonagy, Bateman, & Bateman, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The importance of assessing mentalizing capacity lies in the patient's mentalizing profile and in balance and rebalancing across the dimensions (Luyten et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The importance of assessing mentalizing capacity lies in the patient's mentalizing profile and in balance and rebalancing across the dimensions <ref type="bibr">(Luyten et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, mental health and psychopathology are defined in terms of balance or imbalance across these same dimensions (Gori & Topino, 2023).
text.formatted: In addition, mental health and psychopathology are defined in terms of balance or imbalance across these same dimensions <ref type="bibr">(Gori & Topino, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, the degree of empirical support for the multidimensional structure itself remains less clear.

Existing research uses a wide range of instruments, many of which measure different aspects and sometimes more than one component of mentalization theory (Asgarizadeh et al., 2025), but there is currently no validated multidimensional model that allows the four dimensions to be examined together as a single empirical structure.
text.formatted: Existing research uses a wide range of instruments, many of which measure different aspects and sometimes more than one component of mentalization theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Asgarizadeh et al., 2025)</ref>, but there is currently no validated multidimensional model that allows the four dimensions to be examined together as a single empirical structure.

text.text: In this sense, the familiar statement that mentalizing is four-dimensional contains several distinct empirical claims: that four distinct dimensions exist; that each of them can be measured; that the poles of each dimension represent a meaningful continuum; that balance and imbalance between them can be defined; that the dimensions are organized together as part of a shared psychological structure; in addition, the common presentation of the model as a four-dimensional model may lead to the assumption that it constitutes a closed and exhaustive list of dimensions relevant to a theory of thinking about thinking.

Although these assumptions have played an important role in the theoretical and clinical description of mentalization and have captured the imagination of professionals in education, clinical practice, and research from a variety of different schools of thought, at present, the multidimensional structure appears to still await empirical validation or, reconsideration of its content.

Two recent articles provide a useful starting point for the present article and bring together the perspectives of senior researchers in the field. Hawksdale et al. (2025) pointed to the use of partially overlapping instruments for the assessment of mentalization, explicitly noting that greater clarity regarding construct validity would help in understanding findings that sometimes appear contradictory and assist in developing new measurement instruments.

(2025)</ref> pointed to the use of partially overlapping instruments for the assessment of mentalization, explicitly noting that greater clarity regarding construct validity would help in understanding findings that sometimes appear contradictory and assist in developing new measurement instruments.

text.text: In addition, they explicitly note that the proposed framework for the dimensions of mentalization is not currently supported by empirical evidence. Quesque et al. (2024), summarizing the views of dozens of wellknown authors in a paper concerned with the conceptualization of social cognition, emphasized the need to better conceptualize, name, and differentiate between closely related but partially overlapping psychological constructs (see also : Quesque & Rossetti, 2020).

(2024)</ref>, summarizing the views of dozens of wellknown authors in a paper concerned with the conceptualization of social cognition, emphasized the need to better conceptualize, name, and differentiate between closely related but partially overlapping psychological constructs (see also <ref type="bibr">: Quesque & Rossetti, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: One possible way of holding the two seemingly contradictory positions in these articles is to distinguish between the assessment of mentalization theory and the assessment of mentalization as a target construct.
The theory can be studied using different constructs and measurement instruments, depending on the research question.

For example, a parent with mentalizing capacity may function similarly, or with an equivalent degree of success, to a parent with emotional intelligence (Gottman et al., 1996) or a parent with a tendency to treat their child as having a mind of their own (Zeegers et al., 2017).

text.text: A mentalization-based intervention can be effective even if the score obtained following the intervention is a score of emotion regulation or of mentalization combining all related constructs (Rossouw & Fonagy, 2012; Midgley et al., 2023; Volkert et al., 2019).

text.text: Because mentalization-based interventions lead to improvements in different measures of mental health, we know that they have value even without defining the target construct.

On the other hand, a lack of clarity in terms and constructs not only slows scientific progress but also makes it more difficult for researchers entering the field to become integrated into it (Quesque et al., 2024).
text.formatted: On the other hand, a lack of clarity in terms and constructs not only slows scientific progress but also makes it more difficult for researchers entering the field to become integrated into it <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Quesque et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: It also makes the integration and production of coherent findings across studies in related areas more difficult (Flake & Fried, 2020).

text.text: Investigating the target construct itself requires greater clarity regarding what the construct includes, how it is distinguished from other constructs, and how its components relate to one another (Hawksdale et al., 2025).

text.text: This distinction may help us better understand what is being measured and what changes are achieved during mentalization-based interventions. Gori et al. (2021) note that if psychopathology is an imbalance between the polarities of the mentalization structure, there is considerable importance in being able to assess and distinctly evaluate this imbalance.

text.text: Currently, additional studies examining the empirical validity of findings obtained with existing measurement instruments raise substantial issues concerning convergent and discriminant validity (Muller et al., 2022; Guignette et al., 2025; Warnell & Redcay, 2019; Wendt et al., 2024).

text.text: There is a shortage of economical and accessible measurement instruments that would allow the level of mentalization to be assessed in clinical practice and research (Richter et al., 2021).

text.text: We ask whether this shortage may be related to ambiguity in the target construct itself.

Therefore, the aim of the present article is to adopt a curious, not-knowing stance (Bateman & Fonagy, 2012) and to invite reconsideration of the architecture of the target construct for research purposes.

text.text: Before mentalization became the organizing concept of a broader theoretical and clinical framework, it was a word referring to a psychological activity: "making or construing something in mental terms" (cite, Oxford Dictionary).
Thus, the first type of conceptualization concerns mentalizing as an activity, or verb, with this meaning.
The second type encompasses mentalization theory as a whole.

Mentalization theory developed in the context of understanding and treating borderline personality disorder (Bateman & Fonagy, 2004; Fonagy & Bateman, 2006) and integrated difficulties in mentalizing with additional constructs, such as emotion regulation, attachment, interpersonal functioning, and epistemic trust (Fonagy, Luyten, & Allison, 2015).
text.formatted: Mentalization theory developed in the context of understanding and treating borderline personality disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bateman & Fonagy, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Fonagy & Bateman, 2006)</ref> and integrated difficulties in mentalizing with additional constructs, such as emotion regulation, attachment, interpersonal functioning, and epistemic trust <ref type="bibr">(Fonagy, Luyten, & Allison, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Over time, the theory and its clinical applications expanded to different diagnostic groups and treatment contexts (Fonagy, Bateman, & Bateman, 2011).
text.formatted: Over time, the theory and its clinical applications expanded to different diagnostic groups and treatment contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fonagy, Bateman, & Bateman, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, mentalization theory extends beyond mentalizing as a psychological process and constitutes a broader framework for understanding psychopathology, interpersonal functioning, and therapeutic change (Luyten et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Thus, mentalization theory extends beyond mentalizing as a psychological process and constitutes a broader framework for understanding psychopathology, interpersonal functioning, and therapeutic change <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Luyten et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This distinction is relevant to measurement, as certain constructs may be important components of mentalization theory without necessarily constituting part of the target construct of mentalizing itself (Choi-Kain & Gunderson, 2008).

text.text: Similarly, personality disorder profiles have been associated with the co-occurrence of these psychological variables, and some mentalization scales therefore examine combinations of such variables for assessment purposes rather than to determine the relationships among them.

One example is a clinician-rated scale developed to provide a more detailed understanding of personality disorders (Mentalization Imbalances Scale [MIS]; Gagliardini et al., 2018). Asgarizadeh et al. (2025)</ref> examined the common empirical structure emerging from existing measures of mentalization that had been specifically developed to measure it.

text.text: Following a systematic search of three databases, they combined items from eight selfreport instruments developed specifically within mentalization theory (11 questionnaires were identified in the search, but three were considered unsuitable because they focused on specific rather than general aspects of mentalization).
Their analysis identified a ten-factor structure.
The authors noted that some factors, such as interpersonal mistrust and resilience, may be related to mentalization without necessarily constituting part of its core structure.
This proposition also provides a basis for the present paper.

In assessment research involving general, non-clinical populations, the observation that different psychological constructs occur simultaneously or show co-occurrence does not in itself demonstrate an inherent theoretical relationship, causal dependence, or conceptual identity between them (Cohen et al., 2003).

text.text: This phenomenon is well recognized in research methodology as a "spurious correlation" or the third-variable problem.
A classic illustration is the familiar statistical anecdote of a persistent correlation between increased ice-cream sales and increased shark attacks.

The explanation, of course, is not that sharks attack people who have eaten ice cream more frequently, or that people consume ice cream following an attack, but that both variables are independently influenced by a contextual third variable-increased temperature.

Similarly, in psychological research with general populations, an observed correlation between different measures may arise from overlapping measurement methods, shared general cognitive demands (such as verbal ability or working memory), or environmental background variables, rather than from a substantive relationship between the target constructs themselves (Gagliardini et al., 2018; Guignette et al., 2025).

text.text: Such conceptual conflation creates considerable ambiguity and lack of clarity in measurement, in understanding developmental processes, in theoretical discussion, and in clinical use.

In addition, the ambiguity and conceptual conflation surrounding mentalization theory and its constructs generate a broad and potentially unlimited range of search terms and operationalizations in the literature (Quesque et al., 2024), while the inability to reach a shared conceptual consensus constitutes a major obstacle to conducting valid systematic reviews and metaanalyses in the field (McLellan et al., 2021; Hawksdale et al., 2025).

text.text: The multidimensional target construct adds a third type to this theoretical framework: the target construct of mentalizing itself.

This final term refers more specifically to the psychological process that empirical research seeks to identify, operationalize, and measure, with the aim of establishing and evaluating its convergent and discriminant validity.
The multidimensional model describes mentalizing through four bipolar dimensions: self-other, cognitive-affective, internal-external, and automatic-controlled (Lyuten et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The multidimensional model describes mentalizing through four bipolar dimensions: self-other, cognitive-affective, internal-external, and automatic-controlled <ref type="bibr">(Lyuten et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These dimensions have provided a useful clinical and theoretical framework for describing different modes of mentalizing and for considering flexibility, balance, and imbalance in mentalizing functioning.
Over time, this description has become central to the way mentalizing is presented as a multidimensional construct.

However, when these four distinctions are presented as dimensions of the target construct, rather than solely as a theoretical or clinical framework for organizing phenomena, the term four-dimensional carries several assumptions that can be examined empirically.
This distinction does not question the clinical utility of the fourdimensional model.

Rather, it distinguishes between two different questions: whether the four polarities provide a useful way of thinking about mentalizing, and whether they describe the empirical structure of mentalizing as a target construct.

The following four sections examine each dimension from this perspective, considering how it has been defined, attempts to operationalize it, and questions that remain open regarding its status as an empirical dimension.
The self-other dimension refers to the target of mentalizing: understanding one's own mental states versus interpreting the mental states of others.
Adaptive and balanced mentalizing is described as the capacity to move flexibly between these two perspectives while maintaining a clear distinction between them (Bateman & Fonagy, 2004 , 2012).
text.formatted: Adaptive and balanced mentalizing is described as the capacity to move flexibly between these two perspectives while maintaining a clear distinction between them <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bateman & Fonagy, 2004</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Several existing measurement instruments provide direct operationalizations of this distinction.
For example, the Mentalization Scale (MentS; Dimitrijević et al., 2018) includes separate subscales assessing self-oriented mentalizing (MentS-Self) and other-oriented mentalizing (MentS-Other).
text.formatted: For example, the Mentalization Scale (MentS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Dimitrijević et al., 2018)</ref> includes separate subscales assessing self-oriented mentalizing (MentS-Self) and other-oriented mentalizing (MentS-Other).

text.text: Similarly, the Certainty About Mental States Questionnaire (CAMSQ; Müller et al., 2023) was developed as a two-dimensional measure assessing certainty about one's own mental states (Self-Certainty) and those of others (Other-Certainty).
text.formatted: Similarly, the Certainty About Mental States Questionnaire (CAMSQ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Müller et al., 2023)</ref> was developed as a two-dimensional measure assessing certainty about one's own mental states (Self-Certainty) and those of others (Other-Certainty).

text.text: Validation studies of the CAMSQ provided empirical support for the distinction between these two dimensions and also demonstrated how imbalances between them are associated with impairments in personality functioning and psychopathology (Müller et al., 2023).

text.text: Psychometric literature offers additional complexity and different ways of conceptualizing and measuring this distinction.

A recent systematic review found considerable variation in how different measurement instruments represent mentalizing of the self and others, the capacity to distinguish between them, and the ca pacity for integration and synthesis of the two perspectives (Hawksdale et al., 2025).

text.text: In addition, interactive measurement instruments offer more complex conceptual distinctions.

For example, the Interactive Mentalizing Questionnaire (IMQ; Wu et al., 2022) distinguishes among three relational aspects: self-self, self-other, and other-self mentalizing (Wu et al., 2022; see also Asgarizadeh et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, the Interactive Mentalizing Questionnaire (IMQ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Wu et al., 2022)</ref> distinguishes among three relational aspects: self-self, self-other, and other-self mentalizing <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Wu et al., 2022</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Asgarizadeh et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, empirical evidence is accumulating that distinct aspects of self-and other-oriented mentalizing can be differentiated and measured, alongside diverse ways of conceptualizing the relationship and dynamic interplay between them.
The internal-external dimension refers to the source of information on which a person relies when interpreting and mentalizing mental states in oneself and others.

At the external pole (externally focused), understanding relies primarily on overt and directly observable cues, such as facial expressions, body language, gestures, tone of voice, and observable behavior.

By contrast, at the internal pole (internally focused), understanding is based on attending to and thinking about covert mental states that are not accessible to physical observation, such as thoughts, feelings, intentions, desires, and beliefs (Bateman & Fonagy, 2012).
text.formatted: By contrast, at the internal pole (internally focused), understanding is based on attending to and thinking about covert mental states that are not accessible to physical observation, such as thoughts, feelings, intentions, desires, and beliefs <ref type="bibr">(Bateman & Fonagy, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: For example, one may infer that a person is angry from a tense facial expression and aggressive tone of voice (external mentalizing), or infer that the person is experiencing disappointment based on knowledge of their internal expectations and the personal meaning they attribute to an event (internal mentalizing).
Alongside the clinical usefulness of this distinction, the theoretical and methodological literature raises conceptual questions regarding how it operates across different types of mental states.

As Liljenfors and Lundh (2015) note, there is an inherent asymmetry within this dimension: whereas emotions have both an internal experiential component and a clear external bodily expression, such as facial expressions, cognitive statessuch as thoughts, beliefs, and suppositions-do not tend to have direct physical or bodily expressions.

This analysis raises the question of what external cues correspond to abstract cognitive states and whether this dimension is primarily relevant to interpreting others' emotions rather than the full range of mental states (Jańczak, 2021; Liljenfors & Lundh, 2015).

text.text: These issues leave open the question of how the two sides of the internal-external distinction can be operationalized and measured in a parallel and balanced manner, particularly when the availability of external cues varies according to the type of mental state and the target of mentalizing (Jańczak, 2021).

text.text: The cognitive-affective dimension represents a central axis in the bipolar architecture of mentalizing.
Balanced and adaptive mentalizing is described as a dynamic and flexible integration of the two poles, rather than rigid or one-sided reliance on either one (Luyten et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Balanced and adaptive mentalizing is described as a dynamic and flexible integration of the two poles, rather than rigid or one-sided reliance on either one <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Luyten et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Cognitive mentalizing primarily refers to the identification, representation, and interpretation of thoughts, beliefs, suppositions, and intentions, whereas affective mentalizing refers to the interpretation and processing of emotions, bodily sensations, and affective states (Fonagy & Luyten, 2009).
text.formatted: Cognitive mentalizing primarily refers to the identification, representation, and interpretation of thoughts, beliefs, suppositions, and intentions, whereas affective mentalizing refers to the interpretation and processing of emotions, bodily sensations, and affective states <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fonagy & Luyten, 2009</ref>).

text.text: An imbalance toward the cognitive pole is expressed as a cold intellectual understanding or pseudomentalizing disconnected from authentic emotional experience, whereas an imbalance toward the affective pole is characterized by flooding and dominance of emotional arousal without sufficient cognitive processing, conceptualization, or modulation (Gagliardini et al., 2018; Luyten et al., 2020).

text.text: At the conceptual level, cognitive and affective mentalizing have often been defined according to the type of mental state being represented, such as thoughts versus feelings, creating ambiguity as to whether the distinction concerns the mental content under consideration, the mode of psychological processing, or a combination of the two (Duschinsky & Foster, 2021).

text.text: Thus, alongside existing operationalizations, some conceptual ambiguity remains regarding the organizing principle of the cognitive-affective distinction in the research literature.

The automatic-controlled dimension developed over the course of mentalization theory from early ideas concerning reflective and deliberate processing versus automatic processing (Bateman & Fonagy, 2012).

text.text: This development led to the more detailed conceptual distinction between explicit and implicit mentalizing (Luyten & Fonagy, 2015).

text.text: Explicit mentalizing is described as conscious, verbal, deliberate, and intentional (Luyten et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Explicit mentalizing is described as conscious, verbal, deliberate, and intentional <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Luyten et al., 2020</ref>).

text.text: An explicit process relies on reflective effort and focused attention to conceptualize mental states.
By contrast, implicit mentalizing is defined as an intuitive, unconscious, rapid, and immediate process.
The developers of the theory described this system as "embodied, visceral, and unmediated" (Bateman & Fonagy, 2012).

text.text: The developers of the theory attributed a particularly central role to implicit mentalizing in everyday interpersonal functioning, describing it as the most common and significant core component of human encounters and therapeutic dynamics (Bateman & Fonagy, 2012).

text.text: Expressions of implicit mentalizing are manifested in a range of nonverbal communicative behaviors (Allen et al., 2008).

text.text: An additional distinction that has developed in the literature is between hypomentalizing and hypermentalizing.

Hypomentalizing describes limited or absent use of information about mental states, whereas hypermentalizing refers to the generation of detailed or excessive mental-state attributions and interpretations that extend beyond the available information (Sharp et al., 2011).

text.text: This distinction is consistent with Fonagy et al.'s (1998) reference to underactivation or overactivation of the mentalizing system.

text.text: A related but distinct distinction concerns certainty and uncertainty about mental states.

Whereas hypo-and hypermentalizing refer to the manner and extent to which a person attributes and interprets mental states, certainty and uncertainty refer to the degree of confidence in one's ability to know and understand these states.

The Reflective Functioning Questionnaire-8 (RFQ-8) attempted to link these two distinctions through two scales: Certainty about Mental States (RFQc), intended to reflect hypermentalizing, and Uncertainty about Mental States (RFQu), intended to reflect hypomentalizing (Fonagy et al., 2016).

text.text: These findings suggest that certainty-uncertainty and hypo-hypermentalizing are related distinctions but do not necessarily overlap completely, which means that measures targeting one may not fully capture the other and that theories should consider them as partly independent dimensions.

Similarly, the relationships between certaintyuncertainty and the other dimensions of mentalizing, including the possibility that this dimension cuts across them, continue to develop in the literature (Hawksdale et al., 2025).

text.text: The recent literature therefore offers different approaches to measuring and validating these constructs, including examination of their convergent and discriminant validity, allowing further investigation of the relationships between them and with the other dimensions of mentalizing.
The central question of the present paper concerns the difficulties in establishing the empirical validity of the four-dimensional structure.

The assumptions presented in the Introduction, which arise from the common description of the mentalizing structure in the relevant literature, are:  that four distinct dimensions exist and can be measured;  that each can be measured;  that the poles within each dimension represent a meaningful continuum;  that balance and imbalance between them can be defined;  that the dimensions are organized together as part of a common psychological structure;  and, in addition, that the presentation of the model may imply a closed and exhaustive list of dimensions relevant to a theory of thinking about thinking.

Examining the assumptions underlying the four-dimensional model shows that while the model has a clear theoretical and clinical framework, there is little direct empirical evidence supporting the existence and measurement of all four proposed dimensions as a unified structure.
Although the literature offers ways of measuring certain aspects of mentalizing, there is currently no empirical validation of the four dimensions as a common multidimensional structure.

The degree of empirical support for each dimension is also uneven: whereas operational definitions and measurement instruments have been proposed for some, for others there is no clear agreement regarding how the poles should be defined and measured, and consequently the empirical knowledge concerning them is limited.
It is possible that some dimensions may eventually be found to function more appropriately as theoretical and clinical heuristics rather than as dimensions within a validated structure.
Attempts to measure imbalance also illustrate the complexity involved in translating the four polarities into a measurable structure.

In developing the Mentalization Imbalances Scale, both sides of imbalance were measured only for the self-other and cognitiveaffective dimensions, because of the difficulty of conceptualizing imbalance in parallel terms at both poles of the automatic-controlled and internal-external dimensions.
In addition, within the automatic-controlled dimension, only automatic imbalance was measured, expressed primarily through rapid, impulsive, and non-reflective responses (Gagliardini et al., 2018).

The same mentalizing activity may, at least conceptually, be described along more than one dimension: attending to an unobservable emotion in another person may simultaneously be considered other, affective, and internal mentalizing.

Although the theory attributes importance to balance between the poles of the dimensions (Luyten et al., 2020), a review of measurement instruments indicates that distinction and synthesis between pairs of poles themselves are only partially measured in the existing literature (Hawksdale et al., 2025).

text.text: Thus, questions concerning the degree of independence or overlap among the dimensions, the relationships between them, and how a complete multidimensional profile of mentalizing might be described remain open.
This raises a broader possibility regarding the definition of the target construct.

If the list of dimensions is not assumed in advance to be closed, there is a large set of distinctions that could, in principle, be considered and examined as possible dimensions of mentalizing activity.
Similar questions might be asked about distinctions such as verbal-sensory, emotional-behavioral, or spatial-temporal.
These examples are not meant as alternative dimensions, and they do not suggest that these distinctions are part of the mentalizing construct.
They merely illustrate that mental activity can be organized along many possible theoretical axes.

Which distinctions actually function as dimensions of the target construct, how they relate to one another, and which provide unique, validated, and discriminable information about mentalizing therefore remain open empirical questions.
Mentalization theory has provided clinicians and researchers with a fruitful language for thinking about how people understand their own minds and the minds of others.

Part of this richness derives from the breadth and openness of the concept, which has developed over the years through different definitions, extensions, and reformulations (Duschinsky & Foster, 2021).

text.text: The resulting ambiguity has been a strength of the theory: it has allowed researchers from different traditions to join the discussion and examine mentalizing from developmental, cognitive, interpersonal, psychodynamic, and neuroscientific perspectives [citation].

text.text: However, this same flexibility has also contributed to a blurring of the target construct.
Existing measurement instruments appear to measure mentalization theory rather than the target construct and do not reflect the proposed multidimensional structure.
The four dimensions are not empirically established to the same degree.
Certain aspects, such as self-versus other-oriented mentalizing, can be measured and differentiated relatively clearly.

The difficulty lies in establishing the multidimensional structure as a whole: it remains unclear how balance and imbalance between the poles should be defined and measured, how the dimensions relate to one another, and whether distinct profiles can be derived from them.

This is particularly important as a research problem, because aspects of mentalizing can be investigated without a validated model, but it is difficult to examine the multidimensional structure itself empirically without one.
Measurement difficulties are not new, but the proliferation of instruments and the variation in the factors they identify raise questions about the definition of the target construct.

An instrument may measure an important process within the theory without measuring mentalizing as a construct; therefore, operationalizing the theory and operationalizing the target construct are not the same task.
To date, the measurement problem has been presented as a problem of measurement instruments.

We offer a different perspective and ask whether there may be additional dimensions, whether a descriptive rather than spatial conceptualization may be more appropriate, and whether existing dimensions might be reclassified as clinical heuristics rather than empirical, or new ones added to strengthen validity.
These questions remain open for further consideration, should the field find them useful in the continued study of mentalizing.
